meta.title: BitSpring — free bit-perfect music player for macOS, Windows, Linux and Android
meta.description: A free music player that sends your DAC exactly what is in the file. FLAC, ALAC, WAV, DSD up to DSD1024, up to 768 kHz. EQ, crossfeed and upsampling when you want them.
meta.og_description: A free bit-perfect music player for macOS, Windows, Linux and Android.
hero.title: Bit for bit
hero.lede: A free music player for macOS, Windows, Linux and Android. Your DAC gets exactly what is in the file: no resampling, no system mixer, no surprises.

path.title: Not a single bit changes between the file and the DAC
path.file_detail: FLAC, 24-bit, 96 kHz. Samples are read exactly as stored.
path.player_detail: Doesn't resample, doesn't touch the volume, doesn't mix in system sounds.
path.dac_detail: The player takes exclusive control of it and switches it to 96 kHz, the file's own rate.
path.foot: On macOS: CoreAudio exclusive (hog) mode with integer output. On Windows: WASAPI Exclusive. On Android 14 and later: the bit-perfect USB path. On Linux: the sound card opened directly through ALSA, past the system mixer.
formats.title: From CD to 768 kHz
formats.lede: The player switches your DAC to each track's sample rate. If the DAC can't do that rate, the audio is carefully resampled, and the player tells you so.
formats.dsd: DSD plays natively over DoP if your DAC supports it, or as 176.4 kHz PCM if it doesn't.
formats.files: FLAC, ALAC, WAV, AIFF, CAF, MKA, APE, WavPack, TTA, DSF, DFF, SACD ISO, MP3, AAC, Ogg Vorbis
enhance.title: Want a different sound? Go ahead
enhance.lede: Enhancers are off by default. Turn any of them on and the player's indicator switches from "Bit-perfect" to "Processing" and lists exactly what is being done to the sound.
enhance.upsampling_detail: To 192, 384 or 768 kHz, for DACs that sound better at high rates.
enhance.eq_detail: Load an AutoEQ profile for your headphones. Filters are computed with 64-bit precision.
enhance.crossfeed_detail: Light, medium or strong. Removes the feeling that the music is playing inside your head.
enhance.lossy_detail: Headroom against clipping turns on by itself, and the highs above the codec's cutoff can be gently restored.

faq.title: Questions
faq.lede: Short answers to what people ask before they switch.
faq.a1: The DAC receives exactly the samples stored in the file. Nothing is resampled, the volume isn't touched and no system sounds are mixed in. BitSpring takes the output in exclusive mode and switches the DAC to each track's own sample rate. While that holds, the indicator says “Bit-perfect”.
faq.q2: How do I play DSD files?
faq.a2: Add DSF or DFF files, or SACD ISO images, to the library: BitSpring plays DSD64 up to DSD1024. If your DAC accepts DoP, DSD goes to it natively. If it doesn't, BitSpring converts DSD to 176.4 kHz PCM. There is nothing else to install.
faq.q3: Why does a music player need exclusive mode?
faq.a3: In shared mode the system mixer converts everything to one sample rate and can change the signal. Exclusive mode goes around it: CoreAudio hog mode on the Mac, WASAPI Exclusive on Windows, the bit-perfect USB path on Android 14 and later. While BitSpring holds the DAC, other apps can't play through it.
faq.a4: Yes. There is no subscription, no ads, no in-app purchases and no account, and the app collects nothing. It is open source under the MIT licence; the code is on GitHub.
faq.a5: Yes, on Android 9 and later (64-bit). Get the APK on the download page. With a USB DAC on Android 14 or later, playback is bit-perfect. Older Android versions pass all sound through the system mixer first.
faq.q6: Can I correct my headphones with an equalizer?
faq.a6: Yes. In Equalizer → Import → Headphone profiles, type your headphones' model and BitSpring adds AutoEQ's correction for them. Equalizer APO and EasyEffects presets import too. While the EQ is on, the indicator says “Processing”; switch it off and playback is bit-perfect again.
faq.q7: Can it play on Sonos, WiiM or Chromecast?
faq.a7: Yes. UPnP/DLNA streamers and Google Cast devices on your network appear in the output list under Network players. BitSpring sends them the music as lossless FLAC, and albums play without gaps.
faq.q8: Can it even out the volume between tracks?
faq.a8: Yes. In Enhancers → Volume levelling, choose By track or By album. Every track gets one fixed gain towards −18 LUFS, and nothing is compressed. BitSpring reads ReplayGain tags, measures the files that have none, and can write the result into their tags. It is off by default: until you turn it on, the sound is left untouched.

privacy.meta_description: The BitSpring app collects nothing: no account, no analytics, no ads, no tracking. The website only counts visits and measures page speed, without cookies.
privacy.title: Privacy
privacy.lead: The BitSpring app collects nothing about you. It has no account, no analytics, no advertising and no tracking.
privacy.device: Your music, playlists, equalizer presets and settings stay on your device. The app uploads none of them.
privacy.network: The app goes online only for what you ask of it. The version from this website asks GitHub whether there is an update and downloads it; GitHub sees what any download shows, your IP address and the app version. If you sign in to Qobuz or TIDAL, the app talks to that service alone, and your sign-in stays on your device. When you open headphone profiles in the equalizer, the app downloads their catalog from this website, at most once a month; Vercel, which hosts it, sees your IP address. If you switch on finding lyrics online, the app asks LRCLIB (lrclib.net) for the lyrics of a track that has none of its own; LRCLIB gets the track's title, artist, album and length, and your IP address. Those are the only times the App Store versions go online.
privacy.site: This website counts visits with Vercel Web Analytics. For each page view it records the page, the site you came from, your approximate location (country, region, city), and your browser, system and device type. It sets no cookies and keeps no IP address: visitors are told apart by a code made from the request, which is thrown away after 24 hours, so nobody can follow you to other sites or from one day to the next. It also measures how fast pages load with Vercel Speed Insights, which records the page, the loading times, your browser, system and device type, your connection speed and your country, and nothing that tells one visitor from another. Your browser remembers the language you picked, and that never leaves it. Like any web host, Vercel keeps standard server logs.
privacy.open: BitSpring is open source, so anyone can check all of this in its code.
